paragraphs.source_en:
Oh! there are themes enough for many a bout
310 Of thought-entangled descant; — as to nerves,
With cones and parallelograms and curves
I’ve sworn to strangle them if once they dare
To bother me — when you are with me there,
And they shall never more sip laudanum
315 From Helicon or Himeros*; — well, come,
And in despite of God and of the devil,
We’ll make our friendly philosophic revel
Outlast the leafless time — till buds and flowers
Warn the obscure inevitable hours
320 Sweet meeting by sad parting to renew —
‘Tomorrow to fresh woods and pastures new.’

descant] ‘discourse, discussion’ (Concordance). nerves,] 1964; nerves Nbk 15, MT, 1824, GT.
 curves] Nbk 15, MT; curves, 1824, GT.
 them] MT, 1824; them — Nbk 15; them, GT.
 there,] 1964; there Nbk 15, MT; there. 1824, GT.
 And they . . . Himeros] ‘Then I shan’t need to drug myself with composition or emotional
distractions.’ (GM) S. alludes here to Hippocrene, the spring beneath the summit of Mount Helicon in
Boetia, sacred to the Muses and to the river Himera in the Greek city of that name on Sicily’s northern
coast. Rognoni cps S.’s letter from Pisa to John Gisborne in Livorno of 16 June 1821: ‘Pray, when shall
we see you? or are the streams of Helicon less salutary than seabathing for the nerves?’ (L ii 300). The
nymphs of Himera are referred to in Milton’s Epitaphium Damonis (Damon’s Epitaph) and Helicon
mentioned in his An Epitaph on the Marchioness of Winchester l. 56.
